next_mission_recommendation.mission_description: The current hardening mission secured the application's attack surfaces but left observability and incident response capabilities minimal. The next mission should: (1) Implement structured JSON logging throughout (replacing unstructured string logs) so that log aggregators (ELK, Loki, Splunk) can parse events without regex; (2) Add security-event audit logging — a dedicated audit trail recording all authentication attempts (success/failure), admin actions, password resets, and file downloads with user ID, IP, timestamp, and outcome; (3) Add alerting thresholds — if login failures from a single IP exceed N in M minutes, emit a SECURITY_ALERT log event and optionally trigger an email/webhook notification; (4) Add request ID correlation — inject a UUID per request and propagate it through all log lines and error responses so that a full request trace can be reconstructed from logs; (5) Add a /health and /readyz endpoint with dependency checks (DB connectivity, disk space on OUTPUTS_DIR, session store availability) suitable for use by a load balancer or uptime monitor; (6) Expand the security regression suite with categories M (structured log format), N (audit trail completeness), O (alert threshold firing), P (health endpoint correctness). The mission should produce a StoryForge instance that is not only hardened against attack but observable during and after an incident.
next_mission_recommendation.rationale: Hardening reduces the attack surface but provides no visibility when something still goes wrong. Structured audit logs, alerting, and health endpoints are the natural next layer of defense-in-depth: they turn a silent breach into a detectable event and enable rapid incident response. These capabilities also satisfy common compliance requirements (SOC 2, ISO 27001) that the current hardening work has moved the project toward but not yet reached.

final_report.summary: Three-cycle security hardening mission for AI-StoryForge successfully completed. Cycle 1 eliminated import-path hijack risks (CWE-427) and TOCTOU port-binding race (CWE-362) in run.py, established single-source-of-truth port configuration via STORYFORGE_PORT→Config.PORT→uvicorn chain, and added sys.path security validation. Cycle 2 added secret redaction from logs (CWE-532), weak/default session secret detection (CWE-321), DB path traversal rejection (CWE-22), and output-file path containment in the download endpoint (CWE-22). Cycle 3 completed the hardening with: explicit per-route rate limits on all high-risk endpoints (login, registration, story generation, password reset, file download), Content-Security-Policy headers on all responses, confirmation and documentation of secure cookie flags (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Secure in production), full CSRF protection audit confirming verify_csrf() on all mutating POST endpoints, removal of residual sys.path.insert() calls from web/routes.py and web/admin_routes.py, and a clean pip-audit run (zero known CVEs). The regression suite expanded from 0 to 58 tests (categories A–L) covering all 12 attack surfaces, achieving 58 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped against a live server on port 5100.

key_achievements: Eliminated CWE-427 (Uncontrolled Search Path Element) by removing all sys.path.insert() calls from run.py, web/app.py, web/routes.py, and web/admin_routes.py
Eliminated CWE-362 TOCTOU race on port binding via bind-first _preflight_port_bind() semantics in run.py
Established single source of truth for port: STORYFORGE_PORT env var → Config.PORT → uvicorn.run(), eliminating config-port drift
Added SecretRedactionFilter (CWE-532 mitigation) protecting SESSION_SECRET, API keys, OAuth secrets from appearing in logs
Added _check_session_secret() blocking weak or default secrets in production mode (CWE-321)
Added _validate_db_path() rejecting path-traversal DB_PATH values with ../ sequences (CWE-22)
Added Path.relative_to() containment check in download_project() preventing output-directory escape (CWE-22)
Applied explicit per-route rate limits to all high-risk endpoints using slowapi @limiter.limit() decorators
Added Content-Security-Policy header (default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data:; frame-ancestors 'none') on all responses
Confirmed HttpOnly=True, SameSite=Lax, Secure=True-in-production on session cookie configuration
Confirmed verify_csrf() guard on all state-mutating POST endpoints across routes.py and admin_routes.py
Achieved 58/58 passing security regression tests (0 failures, 1 intentional skip) against live server
Clean pip-audit result — zero known CVEs in dependency tree
challenges_overcome: FastAPI/Starlette session middleware does not expose a standard Set-Cookie header on non-session responses; cookie flag tests required crafting a session-creating login request and inspecting the resulting Set-Cookie header rather than a bare GET
slowapi rate limit decorators apply to route handler functions, not router objects; each high-risk endpoint required individual @limiter.limit() decoration rather than a single router-wide decorator
CSP header needed to be injected via an after_request-equivalent Starlette middleware since FastAPI lacks Flask's after_request hook; implemented via a custom BaseHTTPMiddleware subclass

CSRF token verification in FastAPI is not provided by Flask-WTF; a custom verify_csrf() helper was required that reads the token from both form body and X-CSRF-Token header, checked against the session-stored token
pip-audit required installation (pip install pip-audit) before the dependency audit could run; installed as part of Cycle 3 execution

Some test categories (J, K, L) required a live server on port 5100 to be running concurrently with the test runner; the test suite includes server lifecycle management with subprocess and health-check polling
lessons_learned: Bind-first port validation (open the socket, hold it, pass the fd to the server process) completely eliminates the TOCTOU class of port-race bugs with minimal complexity overhead
Single-source-of-truth configuration (one env var → one Config attribute → one call site) is far easier to audit and test than distributed magic defaults scattered across modules
Log-level secret redaction should be installed as early as possible in application startup, before any handler that might flush a buffered message containing a raw secret
FastAPI/Starlette middleware is the correct injection point for security headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options, etc.) rather than per-route response manipulation
CSRF protection in non-Flask frameworks requires explicit implementation; do not assume framework defaults provide it

Static analysis via Python's ast module is a highly reliable way to write security regression tests that survive refactors — they test structural properties of the source, not behavior that can be mocked away
Combining static analysis tests (categories A–H) with live HTTP tests (categories I–L) gives full coverage: structural guarantees from source analysis, runtime guarantees from actual server responses
pip-audit should be run as part of the test suite in CI, not as a one-off manual step, to catch newly-disclosed CVEs automatically
